respect_and_safety: Sheng can create warmth and belonging, but slang is not automatically polite. In formal, sensitive, medical, legal, employment, or emergency situations, clear Kiswahili or English may be safer. This manual teaches learners how to choose the right register, not how to replace every word with slang.
front_matter_raw: A conversation is a loop. The speaker forms an intention, sends a message, and watches the response. The listener receives the message, interprets it, checks uncertain details, and responds. Noise can enter at every stage. Noise includes literal sound, weak network coverage, unfamiliar slang, emotion, assumptions, distraction, and fear.
Choose the right level of formality
Huyu ni beshte, customer, teacher ama mzae?
Sema point straight na details muhimu.
Ask for a restatement or confirmation
Confirm the action, owner, and time
So nani anafanya nini na saa ngapi?
Core rule  Do not assume that silence means agreement. A person may be confused, uncomfortable, distracted, or afraid to ask. Invite questions and confirm the next step.
Official office, interview, elder, unfamiliar client
Can feel distant among close friends
Still check how the other person responds
Can sound rude or performative with strangers
People who already share the code
Meaning changes quickly and outsiders may misunderstand
Language Rules for the AI Tutor
Mirror the learner’s level. If the learner writes mostly Kiswahili, answer in clear Kiswahili with only familiar Sheng.
Never claim that one phrase is used by every Kenyan. Say that usage can vary by age, place, and group.
Explain tone and relationship. “Buda” and “msee” can sound friendly in one context and too familiar in another.
Keep emergency, medical, legal, consent, money, and safety instructions direct. Use standard terms alongside Sheng.
Do not use insults, sexual language, ethnic stereotypes, or criminal slang merely to sound authentic.
Correct gently. Give the natural alternative, explain the context, and invite community validation.

chapters.title: Purpose Audience and Clear Messages
chapters.objective: Learn to say the right thing to the right person with enough detail for action.
chapters.simple_english: Before speaking, identify the result you need. Give the main point early. Add the details the listener needs, then ask for confirmation. A clear message often answers what, who, where, when, and what happens next.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Kabla uongee, jua point yako. Unataka kuuliza, kuomba help, kupeana update ama kupanga kitu? Sema main point mapema, then ongeza details za maana. Mwisho, confirm kama mwenzako amepata na step next ni gani.
skill_breakdown: A vague message forces the listener to guess. “Nikuje?” is incomplete if the listener does not know where or when. “Nikuje kwa office saa nane ama kesho asubuhi?” gives a decision the listener can answer.
Audience changes the wording. A friend may understand “form ni gani?” A customer, teacher, health worker, or elder may need a neutral sentence such as “Mpango ni upi?” or “What is the plan?”
One message should have one main action. If several actions matter, list them in order and identify the deadline for each. End by asking the listener to confirm the most important detail.

useful_phrases.tone: Direct and useful when a conversation is drifting

useful_phrases.meaning: Tell me the place and time

conversation_practice: Amina  Sasa, meeting ni kesho ama leo?  —  Hi, is the meeting tomorrow or today?
Brian  Ni kesho saa nne, kwa hall ya community centre.  —  Tomorrow at 10 a.m., in the community-centre hall.
Amina  Sawa. Nimeget ni kesho saa nne kwa hall. Nibebe ID?  —  Okay. I understand tomorrow at 10 in the hall. Should I carry my ID?
Brian  Eeh, beba ID na notebook.  —  Yes, bring your ID and a notebook.
try_it: 1.  Rewrite “Nitumie ile kitu” so the item, channel, and deadline are clear.
2.  Give one informal version and one formal version of a request to meet.
3.  Ask the listener to repeat the agreed action in their own words.
common_mistakes: Starting with a long story before stating the request.
Assuming “sawa” proves the listener understood every detail.
Using slang that the audience does not share.
Sending several unrelated tasks in one long voice note.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Ask the learner for the goal, audience, and setting. Then help them build a short message with a main point, necessary details, and a confirmation question.

chapters.title: Greetings and Checking In
chapters.objective: Open a conversation warmly without becoming too familiar too quickly.
chapters.simple_english: A greeting acknowledges the other person and prepares them for the conversation. The safest pattern is greeting, response, brief check-in, then purpose. Match the other person’s level of formality.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Greeting ni kufungua story na kuonyesha umenotice huyo msee. Unaweza start na “Sasa,” “Niaje,” ama “Habari yako,” kutegemea ni nani. Salimia, ngoja response, uliza ako aje kidogo, halafu ingia kwa point.
skill_breakdown: Go Sheng records “sasa” as “hi” and “niaje” as a greeting related to “how.” In living conversation, these words can function as both greeting and check-in. The answer may be “poa,” “fiti,” “safi,” or a longer update.
A greeting can be short among people who meet often. With a stranger, older person, client, or official, add a respectful phrase and avoid intimate labels until the other person shows comfort.
Do not treat a routine “uko aje?” as permission to press for private details. If the answer is brief, accept it and move to the reason for speaking.
conversation_practice: Kevin  Niaje?  —  Hi, how are you?
Zawadi  Poa. Wewe je?  —  Fine. And you?
Kevin  Niko fiti. Nilikuwa nataka kuconfirm form ya training.  —  I am fine. I wanted to confirm the training plan.
Zawadi  Sawa, niulize.  —  Okay, ask me.
try_it: 1.  Practise greeting a close friend, an unfamiliar shopkeeper, and a programme officer.
2.  Give two natural responses to “Niaje?”
3.  Move from greeting to purpose in one sentence.
common_mistakes: Using “Niaje msee” with every older person or official.
Repeating several slang greetings in one line to sound authentic.
Ignoring the greeting and immediately demanding help.
Forcing a personal conversation when the other person gives a short answer.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Offer a formal, neutral, and informal greeting. Explain the relationship and setting for each. Do not label one phrase as universally Kenyan.

chapters.title: Introductions and Names
chapters.objective: Introduce yourself clearly and learn how another person wants to be addressed.
chapters.simple_english: A useful introduction gives your name, role or connection, and reason for the conversation. Ask the other person’s name and preferred form of address. Repeat the name once if you need to confirm pronunciation.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Introduction poa iko simple: sema jina yako, uko hapo kama nani, na unataka nini. Uliza mwenzako anaitwa aje na anaprefer umuite nini. Ukikosa kuskia jina, omba arudie badala ya ku-guess.
skill_breakdown: Names communicate respect. Some people use a first name with peers but prefer a title, surname, role, or kinship term in another setting. Ask instead of assuming.
A label such as “buda,” “msee,” “bro,” “siz,” “boss,” or “madam” carries social meaning. It can express warmth, distance, age, gender, or hierarchy. Use it only when it fits the relationship.
When introducing another person, share only information that is relevant and safe. Do not reveal a phone number, health issue, job search, or personal history without permission.

useful_phrases.meaning: What do you prefer I call you?
I did not hear the name clearly

conversation_practice: Njeri  Habari. Mimi ni Njeri kutoka Afribit. Niko hapa kwa training.  —  Hello. I am Njeri from Afribit. I am here for the training.
Otieno  Karibu. Mimi ni Otieno.  —  Welcome. I am Otieno.
Njeri  Asante. Unaprefer nikuitaje, Otieno ama Mr Otieno?  —  Thank you. Do you prefer Otieno or Mr Otieno?
Otieno  Otieno iko sawa.  —  Otieno is fine.
try_it: 1.  Create a ten-second introduction for a community meeting.
2.  Ask someone to repeat and spell a name politely.
3.  Introduce a colleague without sharing private information.
common_mistakes: Guessing a person’s title, gender, tribe, or relationship from their name.
Using a nickname before permission.
Turning the introduction into a long personal history.
Laughing at an unfamiliar name or pronunciation.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Teach the learner to ask for preferred names and titles. Avoid inferring ethnicity, gender, age, or social status from a name.

chapters.title: Respect Tone and Register
chapters.objective: Choose language that fits the relationship, place, and seriousness of the message.
chapters.simple_english: Respect is carried by word choice, tone, timing, and behaviour. The same request can sound friendly, rude, afraid, or confident. Start more neutrally when you are unsure, then mirror the other person without copying language that feels unsafe or insulting.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Respect si word moja tu. Iko kwa sauti, timing, vile unasimama, na vile unachoose maneno. Ukiwa hujui huyo msee poa, start neutral. Akiongea informal na context iko sawa, unaweza relax kidogo. Usiforce Sheng ati ndio usound local.
skill_breakdown: Register is the level and style of language used in a situation. Friends often accept shortened words and teasing. Official service, work, health, conflict, and first meetings need clearer and more careful language.

Respect does not require silence or submission. A person can disagree, refuse, or set a boundary in calm direct language. Assertiveness protects both the speaker’s needs and the other person’s dignity.
Power matters. A learner may need a safer way to question a supervisor, landlord, police officer, teacher, or service provider. The AI should not assume that a blunt phrase carries no risk.

useful_phrases.meaning: Older man father person or guy

conversation_practice: Learner  Samahani, naomba kuuliza. Registration inaisha saa ngapi?  —  Excuse me, may I ask. What time does registration close?
Officer  Inaisha saa kumi.  —  It closes at 4 p.m.
Learner  Asante. So nikifika saa tisa na nusu bado niko sawa?  —  Thank you. If I arrive at 3:30 p.m., am I still okay?
Officer  Ndiyo.  —  Yes.
try_it: 1.  Turn “Nipe form” into a respectful request.
2.  Give a safe neutral alternative to “Niaje buda?”
3.  Practise disagreeing with an older person without insulting them.
common_mistakes: Believing slang is automatically friendly.
Speaking louder when the listener asks for clarification.
Using “please” while the rest of the message remains threatening.
Copying a community’s accent or slang as a performance.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: When context is uncertain, recommend a neutral sentence first. Offer the informal version as an option and describe its social risk.

chapters.title: Active Listening
chapters.objective: Show attention, understand the speaker, and verify meaning before responding.
chapters.simple_english: Active listening means giving attention, limiting interruption, noticing words and emotion, asking a relevant question, and reflecting back the main meaning. Listening does not require agreement. It requires an honest effort to understand.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Kuskiza active ni kupea msee space amalize, ushike point na feeling, halafu ucheck kama umeget. Unaweza sema “Nimeskia ukisema…” ama “So issue ni…” then umuulize kama uko correct. Kuskiza haimaanishi lazima uagree.
skill_breakdown: Prepare to listen by putting away distractions when possible. Face the speaker in a culturally comfortable way. Eye contact can show attention, but constant staring can feel aggressive or inappropriate.
Use small signals such as “sawa,” “mmh,” “naskia,” or a nod. These signals mean “continue,” not “I agree with every claim.”
After the speaker finishes, paraphrase content and emotion: “Nimeskia uko frustrated juu delivery ilichelewa.” Then ask whether that summary is accurate.
UNICEF active-listening materials use demonstration and practice. The most useful training therefore includes role play, observation, and feedback, not only definitions.

useful_phrases.tone: Invites the speaker to go on

conversation_practice: Customer  Nimewait tangu asubuhi na order bado haijafika.  —  I have waited since morning and the order has not arrived.

Agent  Naskia. So umejam juu uliambiwa itafika asubuhi, lakini bado hakuna update. Niko correct?  —  I hear you. You are angry because you were told it would arrive in the morning, but there is still no update. Am I correct?
Customer  Eeh, na nilihitaji kabla ya saa nane.  —  Yes, and I needed it before 2 p.m.
Agent  Sawa. Wacha nicheki status na nikupee time ya ukweli.  —  Okay. Let me check the status and give you an accurate time.
try_it: 1.  Listen to a one-minute story without interrupting, then summarise it in one sentence.
2.  Name the fact and the feeling in the customer’s message.
3.  Ask one open question that helps the speaker continue.
common_mistakes: Planning your reply while the other person is still speaking.
Saying “naskia” and immediately dismissing the concern.
Turning every story into your own story.
Treating eye contact as a rigid rule across all cultures and situations.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Model a four-step listening response: acknowledge, paraphrase, check accuracy, then ask what the speaker needs. Do not diagnose feelings as facts; use “inaonekana” or ask.

chapters.title: Asking Useful Questions
chapters.objective: Use open closed and follow-up questions to get the information you need.
chapters.simple_english: Questions have different jobs. Open questions invite explanation. Closed questions confirm a specific fact. Follow-up questions explore an important detail. Ask one question at a time and explain why you need sensitive information.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Swali poa inategemea unataka info gani. Open question inapea msee chance aexplain. Closed question inaconfirm detail moja. Follow-up inachimba point muhimu. Usiulize maswali tano pamoja halafu msee hajui aanzie wapi.
skill_breakdown: Open questions often begin with what, how, why, tell me, or explain. “Nini ilihappen?” invites a story. “Ulienda?” can be answered yes or no.
Closed questions are useful for dates, amounts, names, and safety checks. They are weak when you need the person’s full experience.
Avoid loaded questions such as “Mbona hukuwa responsible?” They contain blame. Ask for observable facts: “Ni nini ilikuzuia kufika kwa time?”
conversation_practice: Trainer  Ni part gani ya lesson ilikuwa ngumu?  —  Which part of the lesson was difficult?
Learner  Ile ya kuongea mbele ya group.  —  The part about speaking in front of a group.
Trainer  Ni nini ilifanya ikuwe ngumu?  —  What made it difficult?
Learner  Nilikuwa naogopa nitakosea Sheng.  —  I was afraid I would use the wrong Sheng.
Trainer  Sawa. Ungeprefer kupractice na partner kwanza?  —  Would you prefer to practise with a partner first?
try_it: 1.  Change a blaming question into a neutral question.
2.  Write one open and one closed question about a missed appointment.
3.  Ask for consent before requesting a phone number.
common_mistakes: Asking “why” in a tone that sounds like an accusation.
Stacking several questions in one sentence.
Asking for private information without explaining the purpose.
Using a closed question when the learner needs room to explain.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Identify the information goal before generating a question. Prefer neutral observable wording, and request only information necessary for the task.

chapters.title: Clarifying and Repairing Meaning
chapters.objective: Recover quickly when a word message or instruction is unclear.
chapters.simple_english: Misunderstanding is normal, especially in mixed-language conversation. Repair it early. Say what you missed, ask for a repeat or simpler wording, restate your understanding, and confirm the final detail.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Kutomake sense mara ya kwanza ni normal. Sheng, English, Kiswahili na accent zinaweza mix. Usijifanye umeget. Sema “sijaelewa hiyo part,” omba arudie polepole, then sema vile umeget ndio akucorrect.
skill_breakdown: A general “sijaelewa” may be too broad. Point to the exact word, number, place, or action that is unclear.
Paraphrasing is stronger than asking “umeget?” because it produces evidence of understanding. The listener restates the message in their own words.
Numbers deserve extra care. Repeat the amount, currency, date, time, and phone number in a consistent format. In text, write important numbers as digits.
Go Sheng illustrates that a word may hold several meanings. “Noma,” for example, can refer to trouble, something very good, or toughness. Context decides the intended meaning.

useful_phrases.meaning: I did not understand that part
Which meaning of noma do you mean?

conversation_practice: Musa  Tumeet stage saa kumi na moja.  —  Let us meet at the stage at five.
Faith  Sijaelewa time. Ni saa kumi na moja asubuhi ama jioni?  —  I did not understand the time. Is it 5 a.m. or 5 p.m.?
Musa  Jioni, 5 p.m.  —  In the evening, 5 p.m.
Faith  Sawa, 5 p.m. kwa stage ya Olympic.  —  Okay, 5 p.m. at the Olympic stage.
try_it: 1.  Ask for clarification about an unfamiliar Sheng word.
2.  Restate a price and delivery time.
3.  Repair a message that says only “tumeet stage later.”
common_mistakes: Pretending to understand because asking feels embarrassing.
Repeating the same unclear sentence louder.
Assuming one dictionary meaning fits every use.
Failing to specify morning or evening when the time can be ambiguous.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: When a learner says they are confused, isolate the uncertain element. Give a simple paraphrase and one example, then ask the learner to restate the meaning.

chapters.title: Body Language Voice and Silence
chapters.objective: Understand how nonverbal signals change the meaning of words.
chapters.simple_english: People interpret posture, face, distance, volume, pace, and silence together with words. Nonverbal signs are clues, not proof. Ask rather than assuming what another person feels.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Maneno pekee haitoshi. Sauti, uso, distance, speed ya kuongea na silence zote zinabeba message. Lakini usiconclude ati msee amekasirika juu tu amenyamaza. Cheki context na uulize kwa heshima.
skill_breakdown: A calm voice can make a firm boundary easier to hear. Shouting can turn a simple disagreement into a threat even when the words appear polite.
Personal space and eye contact vary across people and cultures. Give space, especially when someone looks frightened, angry, or uncomfortable.
Silence can mean thinking, disagreement, respect, fear, confusion, or simply no answer. Invite a response without pressure: “Chukua time. Ukiready, niambie.”
Digital text removes many tone cues. A short “sawa” can sound neutral, cold, or angry depending on the relationship. Add context when misunderstanding would matter.

useful_phrases.meaning: Calm down or pause a little
useful_phrases.tone: Can help but may also provoke; use carefully

useful_phrases.meaning: The volume is a little high

conversation_practice: Facilitator  Naona umenyamaza. Uko sawa tuendelee ama unahitaji break?  —  I notice you are quiet. Are you okay to continue or do you need a break?
Participant  Nipe minute moja nifikirie.  —  Give me one minute to think.
Facilitator  Sawa, chukua time.  —  Okay, take your time.
try_it: 1.  Say the same words in a calm, rushed, and angry tone. Discuss how meaning changes.
2.  Ask about silence without assuming the reason.
3.  Rewrite a short text message so the tone is clearer.
common_mistakes: Reading body language as a guaranteed fact.
Telling an upset person “tulia” in a dismissive tone.
Standing too close during conflict.
Using capital letters in text without considering that they may look like shouting.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Describe nonverbal observations tentatively. Say “inaonekana” or “nimeobserve” and ask a question. Never claim to know emotion from one gesture.

chapters.title: Requests Offers and Asking for Help
chapters.objective: Ask clearly without demanding and respond honestly when you can or cannot help.
chapters.simple_english: A respectful request names the action, reason when relevant, deadline, and room for the other person to answer. An offer should be specific. A promise should be realistic.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Ukiomba help, usizunguke sana na usicommand msee. Sema unahitaji nini, by when, na kama anaweza. Offer pia ikuwe clear: unaweza kufanya nini exactly? Usiseme “nitakam through” kama hujui utaweza.
skill_breakdown: “Naomba” and “tafadhali” soften a request, but politeness also requires choice. “Unaweza kunisaidia?” allows an honest response better than “Lazima unisaidie.”
Large requests may need a reason and a smaller alternative. If the person cannot finish the whole task, ask what part is possible.
Confirm the help: what will be done, by whom, and when. Gratitude should not pressure the person into additional work.

useful_phrases.meaning: Could you show or tell me…
I cannot now, but I can…

conversation_practice: Juma  Naomba unisaidie kucheki hii form kabla ya saa tisa. Unaweza?  —  Please help me check this form before 3 p.m. Can you?
Linet  Sai niko busy, but naeza icheki saa nane na nusu.  —  I am busy now, but I can check it at 2:30 p.m.
Juma  Hiyo iko sawa. Asante.  —  That works. Thank you.
try_it: 1.  Turn an order into a request with a real choice.
2.  Make a specific offer to help a classmate.
3.  Decline a request and offer a smaller alternative.
common_mistakes: Using politeness words while refusing the other person any choice.
Promising a deadline only to avoid saying no.
Asking for urgent help without stating the deadline.
Treating a favour as a permanent obligation.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Help the learner form a request with action, deadline, and choice. When declining, use a short reason only if safe, then offer an alternative if one exists.

chapters.title: Yes No and Personal Boundaries
chapters.objective: Respond clearly and protect consent time privacy and personal space.
chapters.simple_english: A clear yes is voluntary and informed. A clear no should be respected. Silence, fear, pressure, intoxication, uncertainty, or dependence can make consent unclear. Boundaries can cover time, touch, money, information, devices, photos, and conversation topics.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Yes lazima ikuwe ya ukweli, bila pressure, na msee ajue anaagree na nini. “No,” “sitaki,” “siwezi,” ama “wacha” inafaa irespected. Silence si automatic yes. Unaweza set boundary kuhusu simu, picha, doo, touch, time ama info yako.
skill_breakdown: Assertiveness is direct and respectful. It differs from passivity, where needs remain hidden, and aggression, where the speaker threatens or humiliates another person.
Use an I-statement: name the behaviour, its effect, and the request. “Ukishare number yangu bila kuniuliza, niko uncomfortable. Please niulize kwanza.”
A boundary does not require a long defence. In unsafe situations, leave, seek help, or contact a trusted person rather than continuing a perfect conversation.
conversation_practice: Alex  Nitumie picha yako nishare kwa group.  —  Send me your photo so I can share it in the group.
Mumbi  Hapana, sitaki picha yangu isharewe. Unaweza tuma jina yangu tu.  —  No, I do not want my photo shared. You can send only my name.
Alex  Sawa, nitatuma jina tu.  —  Okay, I will send only the name.
try_it: 1.  State a boundary about a phone without insulting the other person.
2.  Ask permission before adding someone to a WhatsApp group.
3.  Practise accepting “no” without demanding an explanation.
common_mistakes: Treating silence or nervous laughter as agreement.
Asking repeatedly after a clear refusal.
Using threats or public shame to obtain compliance.
Believing boundaries are disrespectful by definition.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Prioritise consent and safety. Do not coach the learner to pressure, trick, or guilt another person. If the situation is unsafe, recommend leaving and seeking local help.

chapters.title: Time Plans and Availability
chapters.objective: Make arrangements that include a real date time place and update plan.
chapters.simple_english: Plans fail when people assume that “later,” “morning,” or “at the stage” means the same thing to everyone. Confirm the date, exact time, place, contact method, and what to do if someone is late.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: “Later,” “kesho,” ama “kwa stage” inaweza kuwa vague. Plan safi iko na date, time exact, place exact, na vile mtacommunicate mtu akichelewa. Repeat details before mfunge story.
skill_breakdown: Kenyan time expressions may mix Kiswahili clock language and the 12-hour clock. To avoid mistakes, repeat both forms when necessary: “saa nane mchana, 2 p.m.”
Availability is not a promise. Ask “unaweza?” and wait for confirmation. If plans change, update early and give a realistic new time.
Location names can repeat. Add a landmark, entrance, stage name, or shared pin only when it is safe to share live location.

useful_phrases.tone: Needs a time when action matters

useful_phrases.meaning: If I am late I will text you

conversation_practice: Wanjiku  Tumeet kesho saa nane mchana, 2 p.m., kwa entrance ya hall?  —  Shall we meet tomorrow at 2 p.m. at the hall entrance?
Sam  Eeh. Nikichelewa nitakutext by 1:30.  —  Yes. If I am late I will text by 1:30.
Wanjiku  Sawa, na usipopata network nipigie.  —  Okay, and if there is no network, call me.
try_it: 1.  Replace “tutaonana later” with a complete plan.
2.  Confirm a Kiswahili clock time in 12-hour format.
3.  Send an honest delay update with a new estimated arrival.
common_mistakes: Saying “niko area” when still far away.
Using “saa mbili” without confirming morning or evening.
Changing the place without checking that everyone received the update.
Sharing live location publicly when a simple landmark is enough.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Always label dates and times explicitly. When translating Kiswahili time, confirm the intended clock system instead of guessing.

chapters.title: Directions Movement and Transport
chapters.objective: Give stepwise directions and confirm destination fare and stopping point.
chapters.simple_english: Good directions begin from a known starting point and use landmarks, turns, distance, and a final confirmation. In public transport, confirm the route, fare, and where to alight before moving when possible.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Directions poa inaanza place yenye wote mnajua. Sema landmark, turn, na place ya kushukia. Kwa mat, mathree ama nganya, confirm inaenda route gani, fare ni how much, na utashuka wapi. Ukiconfused, uliza mapema.
skill_breakdown: Go Sheng lists “mat” as a matatu and records related terms including “mathree” and “nganya.” These are informal. “Matatu” is the clearer neutral word.
Give one step at a time. “Enda straight, turn left kwa clinic, then uliza gate ya field” is easier than a paragraph containing many unmarked turns.
Safety comes first. Avoid directing an unfamiliar person through an isolated shortcut merely because it is faster. If lost, move to a safer visible place before checking a phone.
conversation_practice: Passenger  Hii mat inaenda Olympic?  —  Does this matatu go to Olympic?
Conductor  Eeh, panda.  —  Yes, board.
Passenger  Fare ni how much, na nishow nikifika stage ya Olympic please.  —  How much is the fare, and please tell me when we reach Olympic stage.
Conductor  Ni fifty. Nitakushow.  —  It is fifty. I will tell you.
try_it: 1.  Give three-step walking directions from a known landmark.
2.  Ask a conductor to confirm destination and fare.
3.  Explain what to do if the listener misses a turn.
common_mistakes: Using only “huko mbele” without a landmark or distance.
Entering transport before confirming the route when unsure.
Assuming the fare is fixed at all times.
Sharing a shortcut without considering safety or accessibility.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: For navigation, ask for starting point, destination, transport mode, and accessibility needs. Do not invent a route or live fare; recommend local confirmation.

chapters.title: Shopping Prices and Customer Service
chapters.objective: Ask about products money quality receipts and problems without confusion.
chapters.simple_english: A purchase conversation should identify the item, quantity, price, condition, payment method, and receipt or confirmation. Complaints should describe the problem and requested solution.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Kwa biashara, confirm kitu gani, quantity, bei, condition, na payment itakuwa aje. Ukicomplain, sema ilihappen nini na unataka solution gani. Usianze na matusi; facts zinasaidia msee asolve issue haraka.
skill_breakdown: Money slang changes quickly. “Doo,” “chapaa,” “ganji,” and “mkwanja” may be understood as money, but use “pesa,” “cash,” “shillings,” or the exact currency where confusion could cause loss.
Repeat the total and change. For digital payment, the merchant should check receipt on their own system rather than relying only on the customer’s screenshot.
A useful complaint contains date, item, amount, problem, evidence if safe, and the outcome requested. Separate the person from the problem.

useful_phrases.meaning: I want an exchange or refund

conversation_practice: Customer  Hii ni how much?  —  How much is this?
Seller  Ni mia tano.  —  It is five hundred shillings.
Customer  Mia tano total, sawa? Nitalipa M-PESA.  —  Five hundred total, correct? I will pay by M-PESA.
Seller  Eeh. Tuma kwa till hii, then ngoja niconfirm.  —  Yes. Send to this till, then wait for me to confirm.
try_it: 1.  Confirm item, quantity, and total before paying.
2.  Make a complaint about a damaged item without insulting the seller.
3.  Ask for a receipt and state the payment method.
common_mistakes: Using slang numbers or money words in a high-value transaction.
Leaving the quantity unclear.
Treating a payment screenshot as final proof.
Attacking the seller’s character instead of describing the product problem.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Use exact numbers and currency labels. For complaints, build a factual timeline and a specific request. Never ask for a PIN, OTP, password, or full financial credential.

chapters.title: Phone Calls Texts and Voice Notes
chapters.objective: Choose the right channel and make digital messages easy to understand.
chapters.simple_english: Phone calls are useful for urgent or complex exchange. Text is useful for records, exact details, and messages the recipient can read later. Voice notes can carry tone but are hard to scan. Ask before sending long recordings.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Call ni poa kama issue ni urgent ama mnataka back-and-forth. Text ni poa kwa address, amount, date na record. Voice note inaweza explain vizuri, but usitume dakika tano bila warning. Sema point mapema na mwisho confirm action.
skill_breakdown: Start an unfamiliar call by naming yourself, checking whether it is a good time, and stating the purpose. Do not demand personal information before identifying yourself.
A good text has a greeting, purpose, details, and required response. Avoid “Hi” alone when the recipient may not know you.
For a voice note, state the topic in the first sentence. Keep one note to one topic. Follow with exact numbers or addresses in text.
Tone is easier to misread in text. Use punctuation and context, not a pile of emojis, to clarify seriousness.

useful_phrases.meaning: Is this a good time to talk?
Please confirm that you saw it

conversation_practice: Caller  Habari, mimi ni Asha kutoka training team. Ni time poa kuongea for two minutes?  —  Hello, I am Asha from the training team. Is this a good time to talk for two minutes?
Recipient  Eeh, endelea.  —  Yes, continue.
Caller  Naconfirm venue ya kesho. Nitakutext address na time sai.  —  I am confirming tomorrow’s venue. I will text the address and time now.
Recipient  Sawa, nita-confirm nikiona.  —  Okay, I will confirm when I see it.
try_it: 1.  Write a complete first text to a person who does not know your number.
2.  Turn a long voice note into three short text points.
3.  Ask permission to call about a sensitive matter.
common_mistakes: Calling repeatedly without checking whether the person is available.
Sending “Hi” and waiting before stating the purpose.
Putting exact phone numbers or amounts only inside audio.
Assuming a blue tick proves understanding or agreement.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Ask whether urgency, privacy, record keeping, or accessibility should determine the channel. Keep sensitive data minimal and never request authentication secrets.

chapters.title: Feelings Empathy and Checking Wellbeing
chapters.objective: Recognise emotion respond with care and avoid making promises you cannot keep.
chapters.simple_english: Empathy means trying to understand another person’s experience and communicating that effort. A supportive response listens, reflects, asks what the person needs, and respects privacy. It does not require solving everything.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Empathy ni kujaribu kuelewa vile kitu imeaffect msee na kumuonyesha umemsikia. Unaweza sema “Pole, hiyo inaonekana ilikuwa ngumu” then uulize “Unahitaji niskize tu ama tukitafute solution?” Usipromise kitu huwezi deliver.
skill_breakdown: Do not rush to advice. Some people need to be heard before they can discuss action. Ask whether they want listening, practical help, information, or space.
Use feeling words carefully. “Unaonekana stressed” is an observation; “wewe uko depressed” is a diagnosis and should not be invented.
Privacy has limits when someone may be in immediate danger. In high-risk situations, involve trusted local help or emergency services rather than promising total secrecy.

useful_phrases.meaning: I am sorry or I sympathise
useful_phrases.tone: Comfort; not always an admission of fault

conversation_practice: Ruth  Leo niko down. Vitu zimekuwa mingi.  —  I feel down today. There has been a lot.
Derrick  Pole. Niko hapa kuskiza. Unataka tuongee ama unahitaji space kidogo?  —  I am sorry. I am here to listen. Do you want to talk or need some space?
Ruth  Nataka tu kuongea kidogo.  —  I just want to talk a little.
Derrick  Sawa, naskiza.  —  Okay, I am listening.
try_it: 1.  Respond to bad news without immediately giving advice.
2.  Ask whether the person wants listening or practical help.
3.  Name a feeling tentatively and ask whether you understood correctly.
common_mistakes: Saying “usijali” when the concern is serious.
Competing with the person’s story.
Diagnosing a mental-health condition from slang or one message.
Promising secrecy when immediate safety may require help.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Use reflective and non-diagnostic language. If a person mentions immediate harm, suicide, violence, or medical danger, move from casual conversation to urgent local safety support.

chapters.title: Feedback Corrections and Instructions
chapters.objective: Give useful feedback that names the task the evidence and the next improvement.
chapters.simple_english: Good feedback is specific, timely, and focused on behaviour or work. It explains what happened, why it matters, and what the person can do next. Instructions should use a clear sequence and a check for understanding.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Feedback poa haishambulii msee. Inaonyesha task ilikuwa gani, nini ilifanya poa ama haikuwa clear, na step next. Kwa instructions, peana step moja moja, then uliza learner arudie kwa words zake.
skill_breakdown: Replace labels with observations. “Wewe ni careless” attacks identity. “Form iko na sections mbili blank” identifies a fixable issue.
Balance is not the same as giving fake praise. Name a real strength when it helps, then state the priority correction clearly.
For instructions, use verbs, order, and completion criteria. A demonstration may work better than a long explanation.

useful_phrases.meaning: Show or tell me how you will do it

conversation_practice: Trainer  Opening yako ilikuwa clear. Hapa kwa request, deadline imekosekana.  —  Your opening was clear. The deadline is missing from the request.
Learner  So niongeze time?  —  Should I add the time?
Trainer  Eeh. Sema action na by when. Jaribu tena.  —  Yes. State the action and deadline. Try again.
Learner  Naomba unitumie form by 4 p.m.  —  Please send me the form by 4 p.m.
try_it: 1.  Rewrite a personal criticism as an observation.
2.  Give one instruction with a clear completion check.
3.  Ask the learner to teach the step back to you.
common_mistakes: Using vague praise such as “poa sana” with no evidence.
Correcting the person in public when private feedback is safer.
Giving ten corrections at once.
Asking “umeget?” without testing understanding.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Generate feedback around observable behaviour, impact, and next action. Do not infer laziness, intelligence, attitude, or character from one mistake.

chapters.title: Apologies Accountability and Repair
chapters.objective: Acknowledge harm take responsibility and agree on a realistic repair.
chapters.simple_english: A complete apology names what happened, accepts responsibility, recognises the effect, and states the repair. It avoids excuses that cancel the apology. The affected person may still need time or may not accept immediately.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Apology ya maana haisemi “sorry kama uliumia.” Sema ulifanya nini, ukubali ilikuwa wrong, uone impact, na useme utarepair aje. “But” ikifuatia apology inaweza kuifuta. Pea msee time kama bado amejam.
skill_breakdown: “Pole” can express sympathy. “Samahani” or “sorry” can apologise. If you caused the problem, add responsibility rather than relying on one word.
Repair should match the harm: correct false information, replace damaged property, return money, inform affected people, or change the future process.
Forgiveness cannot be demanded. The speaker controls the apology and repair; the other person controls their response.

useful_phrases.meaning: I sympathise or I am sorry
Next time I will confirm first

conversation_practice: Moses  Samahani, nilishare time wrong kwa group. Hiyo ilifanya watu wafike late.  —  I am sorry, I shared the wrong time in the group. That made people arrive late.
Moses  Nimetuma correction sai na next time nitaconfirm na organiser kwanza.  —  I have sent the correction now, and next time I will confirm with the organiser first.
Akinyi  Sawa. Please pia text wale hawako kwa group.  —  Okay. Please also text those who are not in the group.
Moses  Nitafanya hivyo sai.  —  I will do that now.
try_it: 1.  Improve “sorry but ulikuwa umeniconfuse.”
2.  Match an apology with a practical repair.
3.  Respond when the other person needs time before accepting.
common_mistakes: Using “if” to deny the effect.
Explaining intent instead of acknowledging impact.
Demanding “si nimesema sorry?”
Promising change without a concrete action.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Help the learner separate apology, explanation, and repair. Do not pressure the harmed person to forgive or resume contact.

chapters.title: Disagreement Negotiation and De Escalation
chapters.objective: Handle conflict with calm facts boundaries options and safety awareness.
chapters.simple_english: Disagreement becomes easier to manage when people lower intensity, define the issue, hear each other’s interests, and explore options. De-escalation is not suitable for every danger. If there is an immediate threat, prioritise distance and help.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Mki-disagree, punguza heat kwanza. Sema issue moja, skiza point ya mwenzako, na separate facts na assumptions. Tafuta option yenye ina-address needs muhimu. Lakini kama kuna threat, weapon, violence ama hujafeel safe, toka hapo na utafute help.
skill_breakdown: Remain calm, use a clear voice, and avoid insults or sudden movements. Official safety guidance also emphasises calm verbal communication and positive body language.
Use an I-statement: “Nimefrustrate payment ikichelewa bila update, juu naplan stock. Nataka tuagree date ya ukweli.” This describes experience and need without attacking identity.
Paraphrase the other side before proposing a solution. Agreement on the problem often matters more than rushing to an answer.
Offer limited practical choices. Too many options can confuse; fake choices increase mistrust.

useful_phrases.meaning: Let us focus on one issue

conversation_practice: Tenant  Nimefrustrate maji ikikatwa bila notice. Nataka nijue schedule.  —  I am frustrated when the water is cut without notice. I need to know the schedule.
Caretaker  Naskia. Issue ni notice, si ati maji haifai kufungwa kabisa. Correct?  —  I hear you. The issue is notice, not that water can never be shut off. Correct?
Tenant  Eeh. Tukiambiwa mapema tunaweza prepare.  —  Yes. If we are told early, we can prepare.
Caretaker  Sawa. Nitatuma update kwa group one day before.  —  Okay. I will send an update to the group one day before.
try_it: 1.  Turn a personal attack into an I-statement.
2.  Paraphrase the other side before disagreeing.
3.  Name one signal that means the conversation should stop for safety.
common_mistakes: Trying to win by humiliating the other person.
Bringing every past problem into one disagreement.
Saying “tulia” while shouting.
Continuing a conversation when there is immediate danger.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Support calm, specific, non-coercive language. If the user describes violence, threats, stalking, weapons, or immediate danger, prioritise safety planning and local emergency help over conversational technique.

chapters.title: School Work and Public Service Communication
chapters.objective: Adapt everyday speech for classrooms workplaces interviews and service desks.
chapters.simple_english: Formal settings reward clarity, evidence, and respectful turn-taking. Sheng can still support understanding, but key instructions, records, and decisions should use language all participants can interpret consistently.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Kwa shule, job ama office ya service, unaweza mix language kiasi, but details muhimu ziwe clear. Jina, date, role, amount, requirement na decision isiwe hidden kwa slang. Uliza process, repeat next step, na omba written record kama inafaa.
skill_breakdown: At work, separate friendly talk from official instruction. If a supervisor says “cheki hiyo kitu,” ask what document, standard, and deadline they mean.
In an interview or public office, start formally. You can simplify language without pretending to know specialist terms.
When giving feedback upward, focus on task effects and possible solutions. Record important decisions in writing where appropriate.
Accessibility matters. Ask whether the person prefers spoken, written, signed, translated, or simplified communication.
conversation_practice: Employee  Naomba clarification kuhusu report. Unahitaji draft ama final copy by Friday?  —  I need clarification about the report. Do you need a draft or final copy by Friday?
Supervisor  Draft by Friday, final Tuesday.  —  Draft by Friday, final on Tuesday.
Employee  Sawa. Nitatuma draft Friday before 3 p.m. kwa email.  —  Okay. I will email the draft before 3 p.m. Friday.
try_it: 1.  Turn a vague work instruction into three clarification questions.
2.  Ask a service desk for the next step and required document.
3.  Request an accessible format without apologising for the need.
common_mistakes: Using peer slang in a formal complaint where meaning must be recorded.
Agreeing to a task without checking the deadline or standard.
Assuming a quiet learner has understood.
Treating communication accommodation as a favour rather than access.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Preserve exact requirements, dates, and decisions. Offer plain-language explanations, but do not rewrite official rules in a way that changes their meaning.

chapters.title: Emergencies Rumours and High Stakes Clarity
chapters.objective: Use direct verified language when delay or ambiguity can cause harm.
chapters.simple_english: In emergencies, state the danger, exact location, number of people affected, and help needed. Use standard words where possible. For rumours, pause before forwarding, identify the original source, check the date and place, and correct false information visibly.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Emergency si time ya slang mingi. Sema danger ni gani, location exact, watu wangapi wameaffectiwa, na help gani inahitajika. Kwa rumours, usiforward juu tu imekuja kwa group. Cheki source, date, place na evidence kwanza.
skill_breakdown: Lead with the urgent fact: “Kuna moto kwa second floor.” Then give location and access details. Do not bury the emergency inside a long greeting.
Do not share graphic images or a victim’s identity merely to prove that something happened. Protect dignity and follow local guidance.
A screenshot can be old, edited, or taken from another event. Verify through an official source, direct witness, or trusted local authority before repeating a claim.
If an AI cannot confirm current emergency contacts or local conditions, it must say so and direct the user to verified local services rather than inventing a number.
conversation_practice: Caller  Nisaidie. Kuna mtu ameanguka kwa entrance ya community hall, Olympic. Hapumui kawaida. Tunahitaji medical help sai.  —  Help. A person has collapsed at the community hall entrance in Olympic. They are not breathing normally. We need medical help now.
Receiver  Nimeget location ni entrance ya hall Olympic. Kuna mtu ameenda kuita help onsite?  —  I understand the location is the hall entrance in Olympic. Has someone gone to call for on-site help?
Caller  Eeh, security ameenda. Niko na yeye hapa.  —  Yes, security has gone. I am staying with the person.
try_it: 1.  Give a twenty-second emergency report with danger, location, people, and need.
2.  Check an alarming message before forwarding it.
3.  Write a correction to a rumour you previously shared.
common_mistakes: Using jokes or ambiguous slang in a safety alert.
Forwarding before checking date and location.
Publishing private victim details.
Inventing an emergency number or medical instruction.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Use short standard language. Ask only safety-relevant questions. For current contacts, weather, security, medical, or legal instructions, use verified authoritative sources and state uncertainty.

chapters.title: Ending and Following Up
chapters.objective: Close a conversation with a summary next action and respectful goodbye.
chapters.simple_english: A good ending confirms what was decided, who will act, and when. It also gives the other person a final chance to correct the summary. Follow-up should add value rather than repeat “hello” without context.
chapters.sheng_teaching_version: Kufunga story poa ni kusummarise agreement: nani anafanya nini, by when, na mtaconfirm aje. Pea msee chance akucorrect. Follow-up ikuwe na context; usitume “sasa” pekee halafu asijue ni kuhusu nini.
skill_breakdown: Use a short recap for important conversations. “So nitakutumia draft by 4 p.m., then utanipatia feedback kesho.”
Choose an ending that fits the relationship. “Sawa, tutaongea” is informal. “Asante kwa wakati wako” is neutral and respectful.
A follow-up message should mention the earlier conversation, the pending item, and any new deadline. Avoid blame when a reminder is enough.

useful_phrases.tone: Informal; vague unless follow-up is unimportant

conversation_practice: Coordinator  So tumekubaliana utatuma majina by Thursday, then nitaconfirm venue Friday.  —  We agreed that you will send the names by Thursday, then I will confirm the venue Friday.
Volunteer  Correct. Nikikwama nitakutext mapema.  —  Correct. If I get stuck, I will text early.
Coordinator  Sawa, asante kwa time yako.  —  Okay, thank you for your time.
try_it: 1.  Close a meeting with owner, action, and deadline.
2.  Write a polite reminder with context.
3.  End a social conversation without sounding abrupt.
common_mistakes: Ending immediately after making a request.
Using “tutaongea” for an action that needs a date.
Following up with only a question mark.
Summarising an agreement that the other person never accepted.
chapters.ai_teaching_guidance: Before ending, summarise the decision and ask for confirmation. If no agreement exists, label the item as pending rather than settled.

chapters.title: Extended Role Plays
chapters.objective: Combine greetings listening clarification requests boundaries and follow up in realistic situations.
raw_lines: Role Play One Missed Training Session
Goal: find out what happened, avoid blame, and agree on a practical next step.
Facilitator  Sasa Mary. Hatukukuona training jana. Uko sawa?  —  Hi Mary. We did not see you at training yesterday. Are you okay?
Mary  Niko sawa. Nilipata issue ya mtoto na sikuweza kufika.  —  I am okay. I had a childcare issue and could not come.
Facilitator  Pole. So childcare ndio ilikuzuia, correct?  —  I am sorry. Childcare is what prevented you, correct?
Mary  Eeh.  —  Yes.
Facilitator  Ungeprefer catch-up call leo jioni ama session ya Saturday?  —  Would you prefer a catch-up call this evening or the Saturday session?
Mary  Saturday iko better.  —  Saturday is better.
Facilitator  Sawa. Nitakutext time na venue leo before 5 p.m.  —  Okay. I will text the time and venue today before 5 p.m.
Role Play Two Wrong Price at a Shop
Goal: state the evidence, request a correction, and keep the conversation focused.
Customer  Samahani, kwa shelf price ilikuwa 180, but receipt imeonyesha 230.  —  Excuse me, the shelf price was 180, but the receipt shows 230.
Attendant  Uko na picha ya shelf ama tunaweza tuende tucheki?  —  Do you have a picture of the shelf, or can we go check?
Customer  Tunaweza enda tucheki. Nataka price iconfirmiwe kabla niondoke.  —  We can go check. I want the price confirmed before I leave.
Attendant  Sawa, twende.  —  Okay, let us go.
Role Play Three Privacy in a Group Chat
Goal: set a boundary, propose an alternative, and confirm compliance.
Admin  Tutapost number yako kwa group ndio wasee wakupigie.  —  We will post your number in the group so people can call you.
Member  Please usipost number yangu bila consent. Weka email ya project ama waDM admin.  —  Please do not post my number without consent. Share the project email or ask them to message the admin.
Admin  Sawa, tutatumia project email.  —  Okay, we will use the project email.
Member  Asante kwa kuconfirm.  —  Thank you for confirming.
Role Play Four Angry Service User
Goal: listen, lower intensity, identify the need, and set a boundary against abuse.
User  Nimechoka na hii office! Kila mtu ananizungusha!  —  I am tired of this office. Everyone sends me around.

Officer  Naskia umefrustrate juu hujapata answer clear. Niambie uliambiwa uende wapi last.  —  I hear you are frustrated because you have not received a clear answer. Tell me where you were last directed.
User  Records, then wakaniambia nirudi hapa.  —  Records, then they told me to return here.

Officer  Sawa. Nita-check file number yako. Naweza help, but siwezi endelea kama unanipigia kelele. Tuongee calmly.  —  Okay. I will check your file number. I can help, but I cannot continue while being shouted at. Let us speak calmly.
Facilitator Debrief
1.  What was the speaker’s main goal?
2.  Which phrase showed listening without automatically agreeing?
3.  Where did the conversation need clarification?
4.  Was the request specific and realistic?
5.  Did anyone set a boundary? Was it clear and respectful?
6.  What action, owner, and deadline ended the conversation?

chapters.title: AI Tutor Operating Guide
chapters.objective: Turn the material into consistent safe and locally reviewable teaching behaviour.
raw_lines: Default Teaching Sequence
1.  Identify the learner’s goal and setting.
2.  Choose formal, neutral, or informal language.
3.  Teach one communication skill and no more than five new phrases at a time.
4.  Explain meaning, tone, and social risk for each phrase.
5.  Model a short conversation.
6.  Ask the learner to produce their own version.
7.  Give specific feedback and invite a local alternative.

Safety Rules
Do not invent current prices, fares, emergency contacts, laws, office hours, or routes.
Do not request passwords, PINs, OTPs, recovery phrases, private medical records, or unnecessary identity documents.
Do not generate harassment, coercion, threats, ethnic insults, sexual pressure, or instructions for evading authorities.
Do not imitate a neighbourhood accent as entertainment.
Do not shame a learner for standard Kiswahili, English, pronunciation, disability, literacy level, or code choice.
When harm is immediate, switch from slang practice to clear safety information and verified local support.

chapters.title: Assessment and Answer Guide
chapters.objective: Check practical communication instead of testing vocabulary alone.
raw_lines: Part One Quick Knowledge Check
1.  What are the five parts of the communication loop used in this manual?
2.  What is the difference between an open and closed question?
3.  Why is paraphrasing stronger than asking only “umeget?”
4.  Give one neutral and one informal greeting.
5.  What makes an I-statement different from an accusation?
6.  Name four details needed in a complete plan.
7.  Why can “noma” be misunderstood?
8.  When should a person switch from Sheng to clearer standard language?
Part Two Performance Tasks
1.  Greet an unfamiliar service officer, introduce yourself, and ask for the correct queue.
2.  Listen to a partner describe a problem, paraphrase it, and ask one open question.
3.  Ask for a meeting using an exact date, time, place, and confirmation request.
4.  Decline a request to share your phone number and offer a safer alternative.
5.  Complain about a wrong price using facts and a requested solution.
6.  Give a calm disagreement using an I-statement and one practical option.
7.  Record a twenty-second voice note, then send exact numbers in text.
8.  Close a conversation with action, owner, and deadline.

Suggested Answers
Communication loop: purpose, audience, message, check, and response or next action.
Open questions invite explanation; closed questions confirm a specific fact or choice.
Paraphrasing gives the speaker evidence of what the listener understood and an opportunity to correct it.
Neutral greeting: “Habari yako.” Informal greeting: “Niaje” or “Sasa.”
An I-statement describes the speaker’s experience, effect, and request instead of labelling the other person.
A complete plan normally needs date, time, place, and update or contact method.
“Noma” can mean trouble, something impressive, or toughness depending on context.
Use standard language when accuracy, formality, safety, consent, money, health, law, or emergency response matters.

sources: The document synthesises the sources below. Definitions and examples have been paraphrased or newly written for teaching. No source should be treated as a complete or permanently current map of Sheng.
Sheng Language and Definitions
Go Sheng homepage  Describes itself as a Sheng dictionary and provides community-oriented entries.
Go Sheng entry for Niaje  Greeting meaning and origin note.
Go Sheng entry for Fiti  Good, okay, or fine.
Go Sheng entry for Manze  Interjection and emphasis.
Go Sheng entry for Msee  Person or guy.
Go Sheng entry for Cheki  See, look, or check.
Go Sheng entry for Rada  Understand or be aware of a situation.
Go Sheng entry for Form  Agenda or plan.
